'''''Capsella bursa-pastoris''''', commonly known as '''shepherd's purse''' or '''lady's purse''',<ref>{{cite web |title=''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/105534/wd/details |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] |access-date=17 April 2025}}</ref> is a small flowering plant in the [[mustard family]].{{r|parnell2012}} It has been described as a [[protocarnivore]] because its seeds contain [[mucilage]], which traps [[nematode]]s.

The plant is native to Eurasia but is naturalized and considered a common weed in many parts of the world, especially in colder climates. It has a number of culinary uses.

==Description==
[[Image:Capsella bursa-pastoris Sturm23.jpg|thumb|Rosette (a), pointed leaves, flowers (c–e), pods (i, k)]]

''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' is a [[ruderal]] and an [[annual plant|annual]] or [[biennial plant]].<ref name="Stace-2019">{{cite book |last=Stace |first=C. A. |author-link=Stace, C. A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=Fourth |location=Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K. |pages=420}}</ref><ref name="Atlas2020">{{cite web|title=Capsella bursa-pastoris (L.) Medik. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020| url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.yes |access-date=23 October 2025 }}</ref> It grows from a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] of lobed leaves at the base. From the base emerges a stem most often {{convert|10–50|cm|4=0|abbr=on}} tall, but occasionally as much as {{convert|70|cm|abbr=on}} or as little as {{convert|2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}}, which bears a few pointed [[leaves]] partly grasping the stem,<ref name="FNA">{{cite web |last1=Al-Shehbaz |first1=Ihsan A. |author-link=Ihsan Ali Al-Shehbaz |title=''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Capsella_bursa-pastoris |website=Flora of North America |access-date=9 May 2024 |date=5 November 2020}}</ref> each up to {{Convert|6.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long.<ref name="auduflo">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/423/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=423 |orig-date=1979}}</ref>

The flowers, which appear in any month of the year in the [[British Isles]],<ref name="CTW">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A.R. |last2=Tutin |first2=T.G. |last3=Warburg |first3=E.F. |date=1981 |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |edition=Third |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0521232906 |pages=56}}</ref> are white and small, {{convert|2.5|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} in diameter, with four petals and six stamens.<ref name="CTW" /> They are borne in loose [[raceme]]s, and produce flattened, two-chambered seed pods known as silicles, which are about 6 mm long<ref name="auduflo" /> and triangular to heart-shaped, each containing several seeds.<ref name="neltje">{{cite book |author=Blanchan, Neltje |author-link=Neltje Blanchan |title=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing |title-link=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing |publisher=[[Project Gutenberg|Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation]] |year=2005}}</ref>

=== Research ===
Like a number of other plants in several plant families, its seeds contain a substance known as [[mucilage]], a condition known as myxospermy.<ref name="western">{{cite journal |journal=Plant Physiology |date=February 2000 |volume=122 |pages=345–355 |title=Differentiation of Mucilage Secretory Cells of the Arabidopsis Seed Coat |author1=Tamara L. Western |author2=Debra J. Skinner |author3=George W. Haughn |pmc=58872 |doi=10.1104/pp.122.2.345 |pmid=10677428 |issue=2}}</ref> Recently, this has been demonstrated experimentally to perform the function of trapping [[nematode]]s, as a form of '[[protocarnivory]]'.<ref name="nature.com">[https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-28564-x Nature - Evidence for Facultative Protocarnivory in ''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' seeds]</ref><ref name="telegraph.co.uk">[https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/earth/wildlife/6727709/Tomatoes-can-eat-insects.html Telegraph - Tomatoes Can Eat Insects]</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Barber, J.T. |year=1978 |title= ''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' seeds: Are they "carnivorous"? |url=http://www.carnivorousplants.org/cpn/articles/CPNv07n2p39_42.pdf |journal=[[Carnivorous Plant Newsletter]] |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=39–42 |doi=10.55360/cpn072.jb538 }}</ref>

''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' is closely related to the [[model organism]] ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' and is also used as a model organism, because the variety of genes expressed throughout its life cycle can be compared to genes that have been well studied in ''A. thaliana''. Unlike most [[flowering plant]]s, it flowers almost all year round.<ref name="neltje" /><ref name="china">{{cite web |title=Capsella bursa-pastoris |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200009292 |website=Flora of China}}</ref> Like other annual ruderals exploiting [[disturbed ground]], ''C. bursa-pastoris'' reproduces entirely from seed, has a long [[soil seed bank]]<ref name="Preston2002">{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=CD |title=New Atlas of the British & Irish Flora |last2=Pearman |first2=DA |last3=Dines |first3=TD |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0198510673}}</ref> and short [[generation time]];<ref name="Aksoy1998">{{cite journal |last1=Aksoy |first1=A |last2=Dixon |first2=JM |last3=Hale |first3=WH |year=1998 |title=Biological flora of the British Isles. ''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' (L.) Medikus (''Thlaspi bursapastoris'' L., ''Bursa bursa-pastoris'' (L.) Shull, ''Bursa pastoris'' (L.) Weber) |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=86 |pages=171–186 |arxiv=1303.1393 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2745.1998.00260.x |s2cid=84689066}}</ref> it is capable of producing several generations each year.

[[Fumaric acid]] has been isolated from the plant.{{r|Kuroda_1976}}

==Taxonomy==
''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' is classified in the [[Capsella (plant)|''Capsella'']] genus of plants in the family [[Brassicaceae]]. It has two [[subspecies]], ''bursa-pastoris'' and ''thracicus''.<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=30092589-2 |title=''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' (L.) Medik. |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref>

===History===
A very early European illustration of ''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' was published in a medieval ''Herbarius'' in approximately 1486. The book was printed in [[Louvain]] in what is now Belgium. The species was apparently not included in the ancient [[pharmacopoeia]] with [[William Turner (naturalist)|William Turner]] stating in 1548 that it and twenty or thirty others had come to be known as medicinal plants from Arab sources.<ref name=Morton>{{cite book |last=Morton |first=A.G. |date=1981 |title=History of Botanical Science' |pages=96–97, 118, 150 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=0125083823 |url=https://archive.org/details/historyofbotanic0000mort/page/96/mode/2up}}</ref>

It was formally described by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his seminal publication ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753) and then published by [[Friedrich Kasimir Medikus]] in ''Pflanzen-Gattungen'' (Pfl.-Gatt.) in 1792.<ref name="POWO" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Brassicaceae Capsella bursa-pastoris Medik|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=279929-1|publisher=ipni.org|access-date=14 December 2017}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
The genus name ''capsella'' means 'little box' and the [[specific epithet]] ''bursa-pastoris'' means 'purse of the shepherd'.<ref name="auduflo" /> [[William Coles (botanist)|William Coles]] wrote in his book ''Adam in Eden'' (1657), "It is called Shepherd's purse or Scrip (wallet) from the likeness of the seed hath with that kind of leathearne bag, wherein Shepherds carry their Victualls [food and drink] into the field."<ref name="Readers">{{cite book |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |year=1981 |isbn=9780276002175 |page=54}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is native to eastern Europe and [[Asia minor]],<ref name="Aksoy1998" /> but is naturalized and considered a common weed in many parts of the world, especially in colder climates,<ref name="pakistan">{{cite web |title=Capsella bursa-pastoris |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=200009292 |website=Flora of Pakistan}}</ref> including the [[British Isles]]<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref> (where it is regarded as an [[archaeophyte]]),<ref name="Preston2002" /><ref name="Preston2004">{{cite journal |last1=Preston |first1=CD |last2=Pearman |first2=DA |last3=Hall |first3=AR |year=2004 |title=Archaeophytes in Britain |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=145 |issue=3 |pages=257–294 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2004.00284.x |doi-access=free}}</ref> North America,<ref>{{cite web |title=Capsella bursa-pastoris (L.) Medik |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=CABU2 |website=[[USDA]] Plants Database}}</ref><ref name="neltje" /> and China,<ref name="china" /> but also in the [[Mediterranean]] and North Africa.<ref name="Aksoy1998" /> ''C. bursa-pastoris'' is the second-most prolific wild plant in the world<ref name="china" /> and is common on cultivated ground and waysides and meadows.<ref name="CTW" />

== Ecology ==
Pathogens of this plant include:{{citation needed|date=April 2020}}
* White rust ''[[Albugo candida]]''
* One species of downy mildew ''[[Hyaloperonospora parasitica]]''
* ''[[Phoma herbarum]]''<ref name="HH&GGE2004">Helgi Hallgrímsson & Guðríður Gyða Eyjólfsdóttir (2004). [https://rafhladan.is/bitstream/handle/10802/4090/Fjolrit_45.pdf?sequence=1 ''Íslenskt sveppatal I - smásveppir'' [Checklist of Icelandic Fungi I - Microfungi]. Fjölrit Náttúrufræðistofnunar. Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands [Icelandic Institute of Natural History]. ISSN 1027-832X</ref>

== Uses ==
[[File:Chopped naengi (Capsella bursa-pastoris).jpg|thumb|Chopped shepherd's purse]]

''Capsella bursa-pastoris'' gathered from the wild or cultivated{{r|fao}}{{r|future}} has many uses, including for food,<ref name="china"/><ref name="future"/> to supplement animal feed,<ref name="fao">{{cite web|title=Capsella bursa-pastoris (Ecocrop code 4164)|url=http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/dataSheet?id=4164|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304193735/http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/dataSheet?id=4164|archive-date=2016-03-04|access-date=2008-08-06|website=ecocrop|publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations}}</ref> for cosmetics,<ref name="fao"/> and in traditional medicine<ref name="china" /><ref name="fao" />—reportedly to stop bleeding.<ref name="Nyerges-2017" /> The plant can be eaten raw;<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=164 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref> the leaves are best when gathered young.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Benoliel|first=Doug|title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest|publisher=Skipstone|year=2011|isbn=978-1-59485-366-1|edition=Rev. and updated|location=Seattle, WA|pages=139|oclc=668195076}}</ref> Native Americans ground it into a meal and made a beverage from it.<ref name="Nyerges-2017">{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>

===Cooking===
It is eaten as a leaf vegetable and cultivated as a commercial food crop in Asia.<ref name="naturesrestaurant">{{cite book |last1=Mills |first1=David |title=Nature's Restaurant: Fields, Forests & Wetlands Foods of Eastern North America - A Complete Wild Food Guide|date=March 11, 2014 |url=http://natures-restaurant-online.com/ShepherdsPurse.html}}</ref> In China, where it is known as ''jìcài'' ({{lang|zh-Hans|荠菜}}; {{lang|zh-Hant|薺菜}}) its use as food has been recorded since the [[Zhou Dynasty]]. Historically, it was used to make [[geng (dish)| geng]] soup, [[congee]], and preserved as ''yāncài'' ({{lang|zh-Hant|醃菜}}). In the Ming-dynasty famine survival guide [[Jiuhuang bencao]], it was recommended to mix ''jìcài'' with water and other ingredients to make bread-like [[Bing (bread)|bing]].<ref>Li, Shizhen (1596).  "Bencaogangmu". Cai Part Two [https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9C%AC%E8%8D%89%E7%B6%B1%E7%9B%AE/%E8%8F%9C%E4%B9%8B%E4%BA%8C#%E8%96%BA] </ref> Today, it is commonly used in food in [[Shanghai]] and the surrounding [[Jiangnan]] region. The savory leaf is stir-fried with [[Nian gao|nian gao rice cakes]] and other ingredients or as part of the filling in [[wonton]]s.{{r|boston}} It is one of the ingredients of the symbolic dish consumed in the Japanese spring-time festival, ''[[Nanakusa-no-sekku]]''. In Korea, it is known as ''naengi'' ({{lang|ko|냉이}}) and used in the characteristic Korean dish, [[namul]] (fresh greens and wild vegetables).<ref name="korea">{{cite book |title=Korea: a historical and cultural dictionary |pages=310 |author=Pratt Keith L. |author2=Richard Rutt |author3=James Hoare |isbn=978-0-7007-0464-4 |year=1999 |publisher=Curzon Press |location=Richmond, Surrey.}}</ref>

== In culture ==
In China, where it is known as ''jìcài'' ({{lang|zh-Hans|荠菜}};<ref>{{cite book |last1=Larkcom |first1=Joy |url=https://archive.org/details/orientalvegetabl0000lark/page/214 |title=Oriental Vegetables : The Complete Guide for Garden and Kitchen |date=1991 |publisher=Kodansha International |isbn=978-4-7700-1619-5 |location=Tokyo ; New York |page=214 |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref> {{lang|zh-Hant|薺菜}}), the term first appears in the song and poetry collection ''[[Shijing]]'' ({{circa|1000 – 600 [[BCE]]}}),<ref>{{cite book |last1=Waley |first1=Arthur |title=The book of songs |last2=Allen |first2=Joseph Roe |date=1996 |publisher=Grove Press |isbn=978-0-8021-3477-6 |location=New York |pages=xv, 31}}</ref> although this may refer to other plants. While today ''ji'' clearly indicates this species, previously it was used for all plants with leaves consumed in soups.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Needham |first1=Joseph |url=https://archive.org/details/Science-and-Civilisation-in-China/Vol.6-4%202015%20Biology%20and%20Biological%20Technology%252C%20Traditional%20Botany%20-%20An%20Ethnobotanical%20Approach/page/15 |title=Science and Civilisation in China |last2=Métailié |first2=Georges |date=2015 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-10987-2 |volume=6 Biology and Biological Technology Part IV: Traditional Botany: An Ethnobotanical Approach |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom |page=15 |language=en |translator-last1=Lloyd |translator-first1=Janet |access-date=29 December 2024 |url-access=registration}}</ref> In a poem in the ''Shijing'', the taste of the ''jìcài'' was compared to a happy marriage.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Legge |first1=James |url=https://archive.org/details/chineseclassics41legg/page/56 |title=The Chinese classics |last2=Zuoqiu |first2=Ming Zuo zhuan |date=1893 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=Oxford |page=56 |access-date=29 December 2024}}</ref> Its sweet taste is also recorded in the ''[[Erya]]'' lexicon, compiled {{circa|500 – 100 BCE|lk=no}}).<ref>{{Cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= |title=Erya – Ji |url=https://ctext.org/er-ya/shi-cao |access-date=29 December 2024 |website=Chinese Text Project |publisher=}}</ref>

In England and Scotland, the species was once commonly called 'mother's heart', from which was derived a child's game/trick of picking the seed pod, which then would burst and the child would be accused of 'breaking his mother's heart'.<ref name="Readers" />
